titulo_es: Participle clauses (advanced: Having been told…, Being the eldest…)
descripcion_es: Perfect, passive and causal participles; clauses with their own subject (absolute) and the “dangling” participle mistake.
resumen: Participle clauses condense a subordinate clause (cause, time, condition, consequence) into a form with -ing or -ed. At advanced level they combine with perfect aspect and the passive voice, and they can have their own subject.

filas: Being the eldest, she looked after the others.
Prior action or cause (after having…, as I had…)
Having finished the report, he went home.
Having been warned twice, he was dismissed.
Passive in progress or passive cause
Being watched by the police, he stayed indoors.
Seen from above, the city looks tiny.
Not having heard the news, I was surprised.
The meeting over, we went for lunch.

explicacion.texto: Golden rule: the implicit subject of the participle must be the same as that of the main clause. If it isn't, you get a “dangling” participle (dangling participle), which is incorrect or unintentionally comic: Walking down the street, the rain started (it sounds as if the rain was walking). Correct: Walking down the street, I got caught in the rain.

items: If the participle has a different subject, it is stated in front (absolute construction): Weather permitting, we'll eat outside. All things considered, it was a success.
Conjunctions + participle: after/before/since/while/when + -ing; if/unless/once/until/when/as + past participle (if asked, unless told otherwise, once opened).
Having + past participle stresses that the first action finished before the second.

ejemplos.frase: Having been told the truth, she felt betrayed.
ejemplos.traduccion: Después de que le contaran la verdad, se sintió traicionada.

ejemplos.frase: Being a vegetarian, he ordered the mushroom risotto.
ejemplos.traduccion: Como es vegetariano, pidió el risotto de setas.

ejemplos.frase: Not knowing what to say, I kept quiet.
ejemplos.traduccion: Como no sabía qué decir, me quedé callado.

ejemplos.frase: Once opened, the jar should be kept in the fridge.
ejemplos.traduccion: Una vez abierto, el bote debe guardarse en la nevera.

ejemplos.frase: The rain having stopped, the match resumed.
ejemplos.traduccion: Una vez que dejó de llover, se reanudó el partido.

ejemplos.frase: Built in the twelfth century, the church is the oldest in the region.
ejemplos.traduccion: Construida en el siglo XII, la iglesia es la más antigua de la región.

errores_hispanohablantes.mal: Arriving at the station, the train had already left.
errores_hispanohablantes.bien: Arriving at the station, I found that the train had already left.
errores_hispanohablantes.nota: The subject of the participle (I) must be the same as that of the main clause.

errores_hispanohablantes.mal: Having not slept, I was exhausted.
errores_hispanohablantes.bien: Not having slept, I was exhausted.
errores_hispanohablantes.nota: The normal thing is to put not in front of the participle; having not exists but is much less frequent.

errores_hispanohablantes.mal: Being finished the work, we left.
errores_hispanohablantes.nota: If the subject is different, it goes in front of the participle (absolute construction).

ejercicios.frase: ___ the instructions, I was able to assemble the desk in ten minutes.
ejercicios.explicacion: The table row “Having + past participle” applies: it expresses an earlier action carried out by the same subject as the main clause. The clue is the subject I, who reads the instructions (an active action) and then assembles the desk; besides, reading clearly comes before assembling. That is why the form is having + read (past participle of read, spelt like the infinitive but pronounced /red/). Having read makes it clear that the reading finished before the assembly began.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: Earlier active action by the same subject: having + past participle.
ejercicios.traduccion: Después de leer las instrucciones, pude montar el escritorio en diez minutos.

por_opcion.Having read: Correct: active, perfect form; I read the instructions before assembling the desk.
por_opcion.Having been read: Incorrect: it is passive and would mean that I had been read, as if I were the thing read. The subject does not receive the action, it performs it.
por_opcion.Read: Incorrect here: a past participle on its own has a passive meaning (“having been read”), so it would say that I was read. It would only work with a subject that can be read, as in “Read aloud, the poem sounds better”.
por_opcion.Being read: Incorrect: it is passive in progress (“being read”), again with the subject as the object of the reading, which makes no sense.

ejercicios.frase: ___ twice for speeding, he lost his licence.
ejercicios.explicacion: The row “Having been + past participle” applies: a prior action in the passive. The clue is that the subject, he, does not catch anyone but is caught by the police, and that this happened before he lost his licence and is its cause. The correct form combines perfect aspect (having) with the passive (been + caught): having been caught. It is the structure of the table example “Having been warned twice, he was dismissed”.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: Passive, earlier action: having been + past participle.
ejercicios.traduccion: Como lo habían pillado dos veces por exceso de velocidad, perdió el carné.

por_opcion.Having caught: Incorrect: it is active, and would mean that he caught someone twice, when in fact he was the one caught.
por_opcion.Having been caught: Correct: passive and earlier; first he was caught and then, because of that, he lost his licence.
por_opcion.Catching: Incorrect: it is active and simultaneous, so it would say that he was catching others.
por_opcion.Being catching: Incorrect: this is not a possible form in English; being does not combine with another -ing.

ejercicios.frase: ___ the youngest in the team, she was often ignored.
ejercicios.explicacion: The row “Being + adj./noun” applies: it expresses cause, equivalent to “as she was…”. The clue is that after the gap comes a noun with an article (the youngest) that describes the subject she and explains why they ignored her. The correct form is being, the -ing participle of be, which here replaces “As she was the youngest”. No perfect aspect is needed because being the youngest is a situation that still holds.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: Being + noun expresses cause (as she was…).
ejercicios.traduccion: Como era la más joven del equipo, a menudo la ignoraban.

por_opcion.Been: Incorrect: the past participle of be cannot begin a clause on its own; it would need having in front (having been).
por_opcion.Having: Incorrect: having the youngest would mean “possessing the youngest”, which makes no sense here.
por_opcion.Being: Correct: being + noun expresses the cause (“as she was the youngest”).
por_opcion.To be: Incorrect: an infinitive at the start would express purpose or a hypothetical condition (“in order to be…”), not cause.

ejercicios.frase: If ___ properly, this plant can live for decades.
ejercicios.explicacion: The card's list of conjunctions + participle applies: if, unless, once or when are followed by a past participle when the meaning is passive (if asked, once opened). The clue is the subject this plant: the plant does not look after anything, it is looked after. That is why we use the past participle of the prepositional verb care for, which keeps its preposition: cared for. It is equivalent to “If it is cared for properly”.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: If + past participle with passive meaning (if it is looked after).
ejercicios.traduccion: Si se cuida bien, esta planta puede vivir décadas.

por_opcion.caring: Incorrect: it is active, as if the plant were looking after something; it also lacks the preposition for.
por_opcion.cared for: Correct: past participle with passive meaning and with the preposition the verb requires (care for = look after).
por_opcion.care for: Incorrect: an infinitive cannot stand alone after if; you would need a subject and a finite verb.
por_opcion.having cared: Incorrect: it is active and perfect, and it is not used after if anyway; it would say that the plant had looked after something.

ejercicios.frase: ___ having received a reply, I wrote to them again.
ejercicios.explicacion: The table row “Not + participle” applies: the negation goes in front of the whole participle form. The clue is that having received is already after the gap, and the meaning is negative (I had not received a reply, so I wrote again). Not is capitalised because it starts the sentence. The card also points out that having not exists, but it is much less frequent than not having.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: The negation goes in front of the participle.
ejercicios.traduccion: Como no había recibido respuesta, les volví a escribir.

errores_previstos.respuesta: No
errores_previstos.explicacion: A calque of Spanish “no”. In English no is a determiner or an answer; it does not negate verbs. To negate a participle you use not.

errores_previstos.respuesta: Don't
errores_previstos.explicacion: Participle forms do not take the auxiliary do; the negation is just not in front of the participle.

errores_previstos.respuesta: Never
errores_previstos.explicacion: Grammatically it would be possible, but it changes the meaning to “never having received”; the card asks for the simple negation not.

ejercicios.enunciado: Complete with the verb in the correct form.
ejercicios.frase: ___ (write) in a hurry, the letter was full of mistakes.
ejercicios.explicacion: The row “Past participle alone” applies: it has a passive meaning and, here, a causal one too. The clue is the subject of the main clause, the letter: the letter does not write, it is written. That is why the irregular past participle written is used. Having been written is also accepted, which stresses that the writing came first; both respect the golden rule because the implicit subject (the letter) is the same as that of the main clause.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: Past participle with passive meaning: the letter was written.
ejercicios.traduccion: Escrita a toda prisa, la carta estaba llena de errores.

errores_previstos.respuesta: Writing
errores_previstos.explicacion: It is active: it would say that the letter was writing something. With a subject that receives the action, you need the past participle.

errores_previstos.respuesta: Wrote
errores_previstos.explicacion: Wrote is the past simple, not the past participle; the past participle of write is written.

errores_previstos.respuesta: Writen
errores_previstos.explicacion: Spelling mistake: the participle has a double t, written.

ejercicios.frase: Weather ___, the ceremony will be held in the garden.
ejercicios.explicacion: The card's absolute construction applies: when the participle has a subject different from that of the main clause, that subject goes in front (subject + participle). Here the subject of the participle is weather and that of the main clause is the ceremony. Weather permitting is also a fixed expression meaning “if the weather allows it”, and it appears exactly like this in the Rules and keys list. It takes the -ing participle because the weather performs the action of permitting.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: Fixed absolute construction: weather permitting (if the weather allows it).
ejercicios.traduccion: Si el tiempo lo permite, la ceremonia se celebrará en el jardín.

errores_previstos.respuesta: permits
errores_previstos.explicacion: A finite verb would require a conjunction (if the weather permits). The absolute construction takes an -ing participle.

errores_previstos.respuesta: permitted
errores_previstos.explicacion: The past participle would have a passive meaning (“the weather permitted”); the weather is what permits, so it takes -ing.

errores_previstos.respuesta: allowing
errores_previstos.explicacion: It is understandable, but the fixed expression is weather permitting; it is not used with allowing.

ejercicios.frase: After he had spent all his money, he had to borrow some.
respuestas: Having spent all his money, he had to borrow some.
ejercicios.explicacion: The row “Having + past participle” and the card's list apply: having + past participle stresses that the first action finished before the second and replaces after + past perfect. The clue is that the subject of both clauses is the same (he), so it can be dropped. Remove after he had and put having + spent (irregular past participle of spend). The rest of the sentence stays the same.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: Having + past participle replaces after + past perfect when the subject is the same.
ejercicios.traduccion: Después de haberse gastado todo el dinero, tuvo que pedir prestado.

errores_previstos.respuesta: Having spending all his money, he had to borrow some.
errores_previstos.explicacion: After having comes the past participle (spent), not the -ing form.

errores_previstos.respuesta: Having spent all his money, he has to borrow some.
errores_previstos.explicacion: The main clause must keep the tense of the original, had to; it does not change to the present.

errores_previstos.respuesta: Having he spent all his money, he had to borrow some.
errores_previstos.explicacion: The subject is not repeated inside the participle clause when it is the same as that of the main clause.

ejercicios.frase: She had been invited to speak, so she prepared a short talk.
respuestas: Having been invited to speak, she prepared a short talk.
ejercicios.explicacion: The row “Having been + past participle” applies: a prior action in the passive. The clue is the original clause She had been invited, which is already passive and earlier than preparing the talk; besides, the subject is the same in both clauses (she). That is why she had been invited is replaced by having been invited and so is removed, because the participle clause itself already expresses the cause.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: Earlier passive: having been + past participle.
ejercicios.traduccion: Como la habían invitado a hablar, preparó una charla breve.

errores_previstos.respuesta: Having been invited to speak, so she prepared a short talk.
errores_previstos.explicacion: So is unnecessary: the participle clause already expresses the cause and cannot be joined with another conjunction.

errores_previstos.respuesta: Having invited to speak, she prepared a short talk.
errores_previstos.explicacion: Been is missing: without it the form is active and would say that she invited someone.

errores_previstos.respuesta: Having been invite to speak, she prepared a short talk.
errores_previstos.explicacion: After been comes the past participle: invited.

ejercicios.frase: Because I didn't know the way, I took a taxi.
respuestas: Not knowing the way, I took a taxi.
ejercicios.explicacion: The table row “Not + participle” applies: the negation goes in front of the participle and the clause expresses a negative cause. The clue is because I didn't know, a cause with the same subject (I) as the main clause. Remove because, I and the auxiliary didn't, and the verb changes to the -ing form: Not knowing the way. Having is not needed because not knowing the way was a simultaneous situation, not an earlier one.
ejercicios.traduccion: Como no conocía el camino, cogí un taxi.

errores_previstos.respuesta: Not know the way, I took a taxi.
errores_previstos.explicacion: The -ing participle is missing: after not comes knowing.

errores_previstos.respuesta: Don't knowing the way, I took a taxi.
errores_previstos.explicacion: -ing forms do not take the auxiliary do; the negation is simply not.

errores_previstos.respuesta: Knowing not the way, I took a taxi.
errores_previstos.explicacion: The negation goes in front of the participle, not after it; that position is archaic.

ejercicios.frase: Having finish the exam, she left the room.
respuestas: Having finished the exam, she left the room.
ejercicios.explicacion: The row “Having + past participle” applies: having is always followed by the past participle. The clue is that the sentence begins with Having, which requires a participle, and finish is in the infinitive. The regular past participle of finish is finished. With that correction the sentence expresses the earlier action properly: first he finished the exam and then he left.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: Having is followed by the past participle (finished).
ejercicios.traduccion: Después de terminar el examen, salió del aula.

errores_previstos.respuesta: Having finish the exam, she left the room.
errores_previstos.explicacion: This copies the sentence without correcting it: after having, the participle finished is missing.

errores_previstos.respuesta: Having finishing the exam, she left the room.
errores_previstos.explicacion: Having does not go with the -ing form; it needs the past participle.

errores_previstos.respuesta: Having finished the exam, she leaves the room.
errores_previstos.explicacion: It corrects the participle but changes the tense of the main clause for no reason; it must stay in the past (left).

ejercicios.frase: Having been repaired the car, we set off again.
respuestas: The car having been repaired, we set off again.
The car having been repaired we set off again.
ejercicios.explicacion: The card's golden rule and the absolute construction apply: if the subject of the participle (the car) is different from that of the main clause (we), it must be stated in front of the participle. The clue is that we were not repaired; the car was. In the original sentence the car comes after, as if it were an object, which is impossible in a passive. The correct form is The car having been repaired, with an optional comma before the main clause.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: The subject of the participle (the car) differs from the main subject and must go in front.
ejercicios.traduccion: Una vez reparado el coche, volvimos a ponernos en marcha.

errores_previstos.respuesta: Having been repaired the car, we set off again.
errores_previstos.explicacion: This leaves the sentence uncorrected: the participle's own subject must go in front, not after.

errores_previstos.respuesta: Having been repaired, we set off again.
errores_previstos.explicacion: Dangling participle: the implicit subject would become we, as if we had been repaired.

errores_previstos.respuesta: Having repaired the car, we set off again.
errores_previstos.explicacion: It is a correct sentence but a different one: it would say that we repaired it. The card asks you to keep the passive with its own subject.

respuestas: Seen from a distance the island looks like a whale
The island seen from a distance looks like a whale
ejercicios.explicacion: The row “Past participle alone” with a passive meaning applies, just like the example “Seen from above, the city looks tiny”. The clue is that the island does not see, it is seen. The participle with its complement (Seen from a distance) goes first, followed by the main clause, whose subject is the island, the same as the implicit subject of the participle. Then come the verb looks and the comparison like a whale. The island, seen from a distance, looks like a whale is also accepted: the participle can go between commas right after the subject it refers to.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: Passive participle whose subject is the island; it can go at the start or between commas after the subject.
ejercicios.traduccion: Vista desde lejos, la isla parece una ballena.

errores_previstos.respuesta: Seen from a distance the island like looks a whale
errores_previstos.explicacion: Like is a preposition and goes after the verb: looks like a whale.

errores_previstos.respuesta: Seen from a distance looks the island like a whale
errores_previstos.explicacion: A calque of the Spanish order “parece la isla”: in English the subject always goes before the verb.

errores_previstos.respuesta: From a distance seen the island looks like a whale
errores_previstos.explicacion: The participle opens its own clause and its complement goes after it: Seen from a distance.

respuestas: All things considered it was a good year
It was a good year all things considered
ejercicios.explicacion: The card's absolute construction applies: the participle has its own subject (all things), different from that of the main clause (it). All things considered is also a fixed expression, included in the Rules and keys list, meaning “taking everything into account”. The subject all things goes before the past participle considered, which is passive because the things are considered. Then comes the main clause in its normal order. The expression can also go at the end, after a comma: It was a good year, all things considered; that is why both orders are accepted.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: Fixed absolute construction: all things considered (at the start or at the end).
ejercicios.traduccion: Considerándolo todo, fue un buen año.

errores_previstos.respuesta: Considered all things it was a good year
errores_previstos.explicacion: A calque of Spanish “consideradas todas las cosas”; in the English absolute construction the subject goes first: all things considered.

errores_previstos.respuesta: It was a good year all considered things
errores_previstos.explicacion: It breaks the fixed expression; the order is all things considered.

descripcion_larga_es: Advanced participle clauses (Having been told…, Being the eldest…, Weather permitting…) condense a cause, a time or a condition into a few words. They are typical of formal written English, the press and reports, and they give density and elegance to what you say. Spanish speakers find it hardest to make sure the subject of the participle matches that of the main clause and to place the negation and the passive correctly.

contexto.que_es: They are constructions without a finite verb that begin with an -ing participle, a past participle or having (been) + past participle, and that replace a full subordinate clause of cause, time, condition or consequence. They can be active or passive, simple or perfect, and in the absolute construction they have their own subject in front of the participle.
contexto.por_que_importa: They let you write more compact sentences in a higher register, something highly valued in a C1-level written exercise or in a report. Used badly, they produce the famous “dangling” participle, which sounds like a serious mistake or is comic because it attributes the action to someone who does not perform it. It is also common to confuse the active and passive forms, which completely changes the meaning.
contexto.cuando_se_usa: They appear at the start of the sentence in narrative, journalistic and technical texts, and after conjunctions such as after, before, once, if, unless or when. They are called for when one action precedes another (having + past participle), when something explains the subject's situation (being…) or when the subject undergoes the action (past participle or having been). Spanish speakers tend to calque the Spanish gerund with any subject, and English does not allow that.
